Lessons.Title: Solve Area Problems
ExplanationParagraphs: Use multiplication to solve area problems in a community garden. A rectangle has equal rows and columns of square units, so its area is the product of its two side lengths. Different choices can meet the same conditions: explain why your choice works instead of searching for just one answer.

Warm-up: calculate 5 × 2, 6 × 2, 5 × 6 and 6 × 6 mentally. Share a strategy after each expression. Adding one group of two changes 10 to 12; adding one group of six changes 30 to 36. Draw equal groups or arrays to show why adding 1 to one factor adds one group of the other factor.

Paint a Wall: Noah has a rectangular wall 6 meters wide and 3 meters high. Imagine 3 rows of 6 one-square-meter tiles: 6 × 3 = 18 m². Small, medium and large containers cover 3 m², 10 m² and 40 m² respectively. Choose enough paint to cover the wall and explain your choice. Six small containers cover exactly 18 m², two medium containers cover 20 m², and one large container covers 40 m². A combination of sizes may also work. There are no prices, so we cannot decide which purchase costs least; the task does not demand the fewest containers.

In a group of three or four, compare different paint choices. Check the total coverage and whether any paint remains. A teacher can annotate a rectangle with rows and columns as each group explains. Every proposed purchase needs at least 18 m² of coverage. Keep leftover coverage in square meters, the unit given in the problem. Before solving, name useful painting materials such as paint, brushes, rollers, a drop cloth and painter’s tape.

Create a Garden uses Three Reads. First read only the situation, keeping the question concealed: Elena needs a rectangular garden with at least 20 square feet for plants, enough soil for at most 30 square feet, and one side fixed at 3 feet. Discuss what is happening. Read the situation again and identify what can be measured. On the third read reveal the question: find possible garden sizes. Work in a group of three or four, agree how everyone will participate, and use tiles, centimeter grid paper as a scale drawing, and poster materials. The paper grid is a model of feet, not a claim that one centimeter is one foot. Write the agreed group expectations on a visible display.

Try different missing lengths: 3 × 6 = 18 ft² is too small; 3 × 7 = 21 ft², 3 × 8 = 24 ft², 3 × 9 = 27 ft² and 3 × 10 = 30 ft² meet both limits; 3 × 11 = 33 ft² is too large. These are the whole-foot possibilities. The problem does not require whole-foot measurements, so other measured lengths may also work. Keep the fixed side at 3 feet and check both limits for every proposal. Make a poster showing the sides, the multiplication, the square-foot area and why it meets the conditions.

Gallery walk: half the groups explain their posters while the others visit and ask questions, then swap roles. Describe a different strategy used by another group and record three things you saw that helped you understand their reasoning. Your teacher reviews the poster, explanation and actual discussion. Correct numerical entries alone cannot demonstrate those activities. Allow a five-minute gallery round, move to another poster after about two minutes, then swap roles and repeat.

Bring the ideas together: a complete 6-by-3 grid, a rectangle with six and three unit intervals marked along its sides, and a rectangle labelled with side lengths 6 and 3 all represent the same area, 18 square units. Choose square inches for small surfaces or square meters for larger spaces; these units are different sizes. Compare strategies that might help next time a side is missing. Finish with a new Edulytics garden problem using different numbers and explain one valid choice.

Optional further practice: Capture Squares, stage 6 (multiply with 1–5), and Rectangle Rumble, stage 2 (factors 1–5), support the area and multiplication focus. Five in a Row, stage 7 (addition within 1,000 without composing), is supporting practice rather than a substitute for the area problems. A teacher may introduce the community-garden setting through an appropriate read-aloud; no book text or illustrations are included here.

KeyConcepts.Title: Area from side lengths
KeyConcepts.Definition: Area measures the surface covered by equal-size square units.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Multiply side lengths in the same unit and name the corresponding square unit.
KeyConcepts.Example: A 6 m by 3 m wall covers 18 m², not 18 m.

KeyConcepts.Title: More than one purchase can work
KeyConcepts.Definition: A purchase is sufficient when its total coverage reaches the required wall area.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Add the coverage of every container; do not invent prices or an optimization requirement.
KeyConcepts.Example: Six small containers, two medium containers, or one large container can each cover the 18 m² wall.

KeyConcepts.Title: Both garden limits matter
KeyConcepts.Definition: A missing side must make the area large enough for the plants and small enough for the available soil.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Keep one side at 3 ft and check that the product is at least 20 ft² and at most 30 ft².
KeyConcepts.Example: 3 ft by 7 ft covers 21 ft²; 3 ft by 10 ft covers 30 ft². Both work.

KeyConcepts.Title: Explain and compare representations
KeyConcepts.Definition: A model shows how the side lengths and area relate.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Label side lengths and square units; explain another strategy and record three observations from the gallery walk.
KeyConcepts.Example: A 6-column, 3-row grid has 18 squares even when only its outside edge remains visible.

WorkedExamples.Title: One more equal group
WorkedExamples.Question: How does 6 × 6 relate to 5 × 6?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the product you know and add one group.
WorkedExamples.Check: Six groups of six have the same total as five groups plus six.

WorkedExamples.Title: Choose enough paint
WorkedExamples.Question: Compare three possible purchases for the 6 m by 3 m wall.
WorkedExamples.Method: Find the wall area, then check each purchase against it.
Steps: Six small containers cover 6 × 3 = 18 m², leaving no unused coverage.
Two medium containers cover 2 × 10 = 20 m², leaving 2 m².
One large container covers 40 m², leaving 22 m².
Explain which you choose; prices are not supplied.
WorkedExamples.Answer: All three purchases provide enough paint. Other sufficient combinations can also be valid.
WorkedExamples.Check: Five small containers cover only 15 m² and do not work. One medium plus three small covers 19 m² and does work.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find possible garden lengths
WorkedExamples.Question: One side is 3 ft. Which whole-foot other sides meet the 20–30 ft² garden limits?
WorkedExamples.Method: Multiply the fixed side by candidate lengths and check both limits.
Steps: Draw and label a chosen rectangle, then explain it on your group poster.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Whole-foot other sides 7, 8, 9 and 10 ft work. Other measured lengths may also work; there is no single required garden.
WorkedExamples.Check: Keep one side at 3 ft. Neither a correct area with a different fixed side nor a length that exceeds 30 ft² satisfies all conditions.

WorkedExamples.Title: A new Edulytics garden check
WorkedExamples.Question: A separate planter is 2 ft wide and must cover at least 12 ft² but no more than 18 ft². Give one possible other side and explain.
Steps: Try an other side of 7 ft.
14 is at least 12 and no more than 18.
Draw and label the planter and state why it fits both limits.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 7 ft is one valid choice; 6, 8 and 9 ft also work.
WorkedExamples.Check: 5 ft is too short; 10 ft is too long. The drawing and explanation require teacher review.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Adding 6 and 3 to find the wall area.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Adding two side lengths does not count the square units inside the wall.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use 6 × 3 = 18 m² and check with rows and columns.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Accepting only two medium containers, or calling one option cheapest.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Several purchases cover the wall and no prices are given.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check total coverage and explain the choice without adding an unstated requirement.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Allowing 6 ft or 11 ft as the other garden side.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Their areas are 18 ft² and 33 ft², outside the required 20–30 ft² range.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check both area limits while keeping the 3-foot side fixed.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Saying only a 3 ft by 8 ft garden is possible.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Several other lengths meet the same conditions.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Find and compare different valid rectangles; whole-foot examples are not the only possible measurements.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Confusing meters, square meters, feet and square feet.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Side lengths and covered area use different kinds of units, and different unit sizes cannot be interchanged.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use m² for wall coverage, ft for garden sides, and ft² for garden area.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating a correct number as a completed gallery walk.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A numerical check cannot assess a poster, explanation or observed peer strategy.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Show the work to your teacher, compare strategies, and write three specific observations.

SummaryPoints: Adding one equal group explains the related multiplication facts.
Rectangle area is side length × side length, with square units.
An 18 m² wall has several sufficient paint purchases using 3, 10 and 40 m² containers.
Keep the garden side at 3 ft and meet both the 20 ft² minimum and 30 ft² maximum.
Whole-foot other sides 7, 8, 9 and 10 ft work; do not impose a whole-foot restriction on the original problem.
Use a labelled poster, compare a different group strategy, and record three observations.
Your teacher reviews reasoning and group work even when the numerical part is correct.
